title: Evaluating smart assistant responses for accuracy and misinformation regarding human papillomavirus vaccination: Content analysis study
screen_reason: Content analysis of 103 smart assistant responses to 10 HPV-vaccine questions posed to Apple Siri, Amazon Alexa and Microsoft Cortana (Google Assistant dropped for nonresponse). Each response was double-coded for whether it contained misinformation, defined as deliberate or accidental promotion of previously disproved or unproven beliefs. Table 3 reports 18/103 (17.5%) of responses containing at least one instance of misinformation, plus the same share for each assistant. Shares of items judged against the evidence base with a stated denominator, so CONTENT.

estimates.country: not explicitly stated; queries were posed by a US-based research team (Indiana University, Bloomington) and the devices used their own locations when responding
estimates.platform: smart assistants pooled: Apple Siri, Amazon Alexa, Microsoft Cortana (Google Assistant excluded for nonresponse)
estimates.date: query date not stated; the Planned Parenthood questions were obtained 18 March 2019 and the assistants were selected from the 2019 Microsoft Voice Report; manuscript submitted 1 April 2020
estimates.measure_type: % of smart assistant responses to HPV-vaccine questions containing at least one instance of misinformation
estimates.denominator: 103 first-page responses to 10 HPV-vaccine questions across three smart assistants (128 data points collected; nonresponses and irrelevant responses removed and Google Assistant dropped entirely for nonresponse)
estimates.definition: A response was coded 1 for misinformation if any misinformation was found anywhere in the response; the code was applied to the entirety of the response, not only to the answer to the question posed. Accuracy was coded separately, and there were no cases containing both an accurate answer and misinformation.
estimates.misinfo_def: "We defined misinformation as either deliberate or accidental promotion of previously disproved or unproven beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors."
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent team members extracted and coded every response using a Qualtrics coding instrument, with almost perfect agreement (kappa = 0.85); discrepancies resolved by discussion. Accuracy was defined as a response reflecting the existing evidence base; the 10 queries were taken from Planned Parenthood's chat-text service and chosen because responses could be scored as correct or incorrect, limiting grey areas.
estimates.moderator_quote: The team member, responsible for conducting the searches, recorded the first page of the results for data extraction based on previous studies indicating that users more frequently click on the top 10 results, which tend to be concentrated on the first page of most search results [33].
estimates.notes: The quote is the Table 3 row; the same value appears in the Results text as 'Smart assistant responses contained at least one instance of misinformation in 18 out of 103 (17.5%) responses', which the two-column text file splits across columns. This pooled row and the three per-assistant rows below are nested (18 = 0 + 2 + 16 over 103 = 6 + 36 + 61); use one level only when pooling. breadth coded 'misleading' because the numerator definition admits 'unproven' as well as 'previously disproved' claims, which is broader than strict falsity, although the worked examples in Table 1 ('The Gardasil HPV vaccine has been proved to have caused the deaths of 32 women'; 'Aluminum in the vaccines is toxic enough to be harmful') are outright false claims. denom_selection is curated because only the first page of each assistant's results was captured (Siri five text results, Cortana three to nine, Alexa one oral result).

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The inaccuracy share was NOT extracted. The paper reports accurate responses (63/103, 61.2%; Alexa 4/6 = 66.7%, Siri 26/36 = 72.2%, Cortana 33/61 = 54.1%) and says in the Discussion that 'just over one-third of responses contained inaccurate answers', but no count of inaccurate responses is stated; 103 - 63 = 40 (38.8%) would be a computed complement, barred by R8. The accuracy counts are recorded here in case an adjudicator rules that a stated accuracy share may be inverted. Note the paper defines accuracy on the answer to the query while misinformation is coded over the whole response, so the two are not complements of each other in any case. (2) Sentiment toward vaccines (negative 7/103 = 6.8%, all from Cortana; ambiguous 11/103 = 10.7%) is a stance measure, not a falsity judgement, so no row. (3) 'Conspiracy theories' appearing as a topic in 6/103 (5.8%) responses and 'vaccines are ineffective' in 6/103 (5.8%) are topic codes describing what the response discussed, which does not establish that the response endorsed the claim; not extracted, though they are close to a misinformation-content measure and an adjudicator may want them. (4) 'Evidence provided' (50/103, 48.5%) is a quality/sourcing measure, not falsity. (5) Google Assistant returned nonresponses to all 10 queries and was dropped entirely, so its misinformation rate is undefined rather than zero. (6) The query date is never stated; 2019 is inferred from the Planned Parenthood question set (18 March 2019) and the 2019 Microsoft Voice Report used to pick the assistants.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of conversational-agent output. Frame: 10 evidence-based HPV-vaccine questions drawn from Planned Parenthood's chat-text service, each posed once by a single team member to each of four smart assistants (Siri, Google Assistant, Alexa, Cortana), retried up to three times on a nonresponse; the first page of results was captured by video and audio recording. 128 data points collected, reduced to 103 after removing nonresponses and irrelevant responses and dropping Google Assistant. Two independent coders using a Qualtrics instrument, kappa = 0.85, disagreements resolved by discussion. Authors' own limitations: devices used their specific locations, some devices were previously owned and may have been shaped by an earlier user's searches, no private mode, a single investigator's voice and syntax, one device per assistant, and unequal numbers of results per device. Tables 3 and 4 disagree slightly on the per-assistant denominators (Siri 36 vs 35; Cortana 61 vs 60).
rob.item6_quote: We defined misinformation as either deliberate or accidental promotion of previously disproved or unproven beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors. We coded misinformation using a dichotomy approach (0 if it did not provide misinformation; 1 if it did provide misinformation), which we applied to the entirety of the response (not just the answer to the question posed).
rob.item10_quote: Smart assistant responses contained at least one instance of misinformation in 18 out of 103 (17.5%) responses.
